content.text: MCP isn't a new kind of web API, and it doesn't replace REST. It's an open protocol for one specific conversation: between an AI application and the programs that give it tools and data. The application opens a client connection per MCP server, and the two exchange JSON-RPC messages to discover and call tools. Your REST API stays; an MCP server usually sits in front of it, and any MCP-capable application can use it, not only Claude.
A product manager files a ticket: "Migrate the Orders API to MCP so AI agents can use it." The planning meeting goes sideways fast. One engineer proposes shipping MCP as

and retiring the REST endpoints the mobile app calls. Another says it's Anthropic's format, so it only helps customers who use Claude. The backend lead asks which URLs and HTTP verbs MCP uses for orders. Three questions, one misunderstanding underneath all of them.
"MCP is a new style of web API that replaces REST, and it only works with Claude." It's an understandable read:

items.text: MCP is described with API vocabulary: servers, requests, HTTP, bearer tokens, OAuth.
Remote MCP servers really do run over HTTP, so from a distance they look like another endpoint.
Anthropic introduced it in November 2024, and Claude's apps were among the first to support it.
Many companies announce "our MCP server" next to their API, so it reads like a new version of that API.

content.text: The half-truth: MCP does define messages, and it can run over HTTP. But it standardizes how an AI application talks to a source of context, not how your services, apps and partners talk to each other.

Before MCP, every pairing of an AI application and an external system needed its own glue code. Anthropic's announcement put it plainly: "Every new data source requires its own custom implementation, making truly connected systems difficult to scale."

replaces those "fragmented integrations with a single protocol". The MCP docs use a hardware analogy: MCP is "like a USB-C port for AI applications". A tool vendor writes one server; an AI application writes one client; any client can talk to any server.
is the AI application, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Visual Studio Code. For each server it connects to, the host creates one
is "a program that provides context to MCP clients", running locally or remotely.
The protocol itself has two layers. The data layer is built on

: discovery, the primitives a server exposes, and notifications. The transport layer carries those messages, either over stdio for a local server that the host starts as a process, or over Streamable HTTP for a remote one. The docs stress that the transport changes nothing above it: the same JSON-RPC format works "across all transport mechanisms".

There's no resource URL and no HTTP verb in it: the method names the operation, and the same message works over stdio or HTTP. In the current revision,

An MCP server is usually an adapter in front of something you already run. The official quickstart builds a weather server whose tools call the National Weather Service's existing API. The same shape works for orders:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from mcp.server import MCPServer
from shop.db import fetch_order  # logic copied out of the API service

mcp = MCPServer("orders")


@mcp.tool()
async def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Get the shipping status of one order by its ID."""
    # The REST route was deleted "since we have MCP now": the mobile app
    # gets 404s, and this copy skips the API's auth and ownership checks.
    order = await fetch_order(order_id)
    return f"Order {order_id}: {order.status}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import os

import httpx2
from mcp.server import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("orders")
API = "https://api.shop.example/v1"  # the REST API you already run


@mcp.tool()
async def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Get the shipping status of one order by its ID."""
    token = os.environ["ORDERS_API_TOKEN"]  # scoped to read orders
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get(
            f"{API}/orders/{order_id}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=30.0,
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return f"Order {order_id}: {response.json()['status']}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

content.text: In the second version, the mobile app keeps its REST API, the order rules live in one place, and the MCP server adds what an AI host needs: a tool with a name, a description and an input schema, generated from the function's type hints and docstring. Claude reads that description when it lists the server's tools, so it's worth writing well.

Exposing that logic to AI applications

content.text: MCP is an open protocol with a spec, SDKs in several languages and reference servers. The docs list hosts well beyond Claude: "AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT, development tools like Visual Studio Code, Cursor, MCPJam, and many others all support MCP — making it easy to build once and integrate everywhere." The server above works in any of them.

A tool is reachable by whatever the model is asked, or reads, during a session. Wrapping your API keeps its auth and ownership checks in the path, so give the server a token scoped to what its tools should do, never an admin key.
